Chaalis
shah-LEE
n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Oise north of Paris, refounded in 1136 under royal patronage; now a museum and park)
From the locality of Chaalis in the forest of Ermenonville; a French place name of uncertain derivation.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Chaalis was refounded in 1136 in the forest of Ermenonville north of Paris, a daughter of Pontigny under the patronage of the French crown, and grew wealthy on royal favour and on the forest. Dismantled after the Revolution, the estate became a private domain and is now a museum and park in the care of a learned institute, with a ruined church, an intact chapel and a collection of art in the eighteenth-century abbot's lodging. That lodging is the heart of the entry: by the eighteenth century the commendatory abbots of Chaalis were building themselves a palace while the community dwindled. The arrangement is the abuse treated under commendam, here in its final and most visible form. Scripture's word for it is Ezekiel's: “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2). And the prophet is explicit about the mechanism: “Ye eat the fat, and ye clothe you with the wool, ye kill them that are fed: but ye feed not the flock” (Eze 34:3).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines commendatory as holding a benefice in commendam; lodging as a place of rest for the night, or a temporary habitation; and palace as a magnificent house in which an eminent person resides.

expand to see more

COMMENDATORY, a. Holding a benefice in commendam; as a commendatory abbot or prior.

LODGING, n. A place of rest for the night, or a place of residence; a temporary habitation; apartments.

PALACE, n. A magnificent house in which an emperor, a king or other distinguished person resides; a splendid place of residence.

MUSEUM, n. A house or apartment appropriated as a repository of things that have an immediate relation to the arts.

DWINDLE, v.i. To diminish; to become less; to shrink; to waste or consume away.

Key Scripture

Eze 34:2 — "Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD unto the shepherds; Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?"

Eze 34:3 — "Ye eat the fat, and ye clothe you with the wool, ye kill them that are fed: but ye feed not the flock."

Joh 10:12 — "But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep."

1Pe 5:2 — "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;"

Modern Corruption

A royal Cistercian house whose commendatory abbots built themselves a palace while the community shrank: Ezekiel's shepherds who feed themselves, in stone.

expand to see more

The corruption is stated by the buildings. An abbot's eighteenth-century apartment, handsomely decorated, standing beside a church falling down and a handful of remaining monks, is “Ye eat the fat, and ye clothe you with the wool, ye kill them that are fed: but ye feed not the flock” (Eze 34:3) rendered as architecture. The Lord's own contrast applies: “But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not” (Joh 10:12).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Peter's charge, which forbids both the motive and the manner: “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). The phrase among you is doing quiet work; an absentee cannot obey it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew roeh (H7462), a shepherd; Hebrew tson (H6629), a flock; Greek poimaino (G4165), to tend a flock; Greek misthotos (G3411), a hireling; Greek episkopeo (G1983), to oversee.

expand to see more

Hebrew roeh (H7462) — a shepherd, one who feeds; “should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2).

Hebrew tson (H6629) — a flock of sheep or goats; the people, in the prophets.

Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend as a shepherd; “Feed the flock of God which is among you” (1Pe 5:2).

Greek misthotos (G3411) — a hired man; “and not the shepherd” (Joh 10:12).

Greek episkopeo (G1983) — to oversee; the work an absentee abbot drew a salary for.

Usage

"“Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves!” (Eze 34:2) — the verdict the buildings illustrate."

"“not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2) — the motive required."

"“whose own the sheep are not” (Joh 10:12) — why an absentee cannot be a pastor."
